text:
process over goals | Inkuary #1

I saw a good romeo meme today about the new year and setting intentions on processes vs setting them on goals. Goals are meaningless! Plans are stupid! I feel like I’ve heard Joe Hudson say something to the same effect: you own your actions but not the outcome, and the Baghavad Gita and the Stoics probably say something like this too. I don’t know why it hadn’t hit me until now but this time it resonated like a gong. Or a bell. ^1

https://t.co/wrghYUwob6

About process. It makes sense to me because of manifesting. Specifically because of how it hooks into manifesting. When manifesting you’re hacking into the active inference loop. Active Inference says actions and predictions are the same kind of thing. Not quite but this will have to do for now. What this means is that usually if you’re here and you visualize yourself over there, your whole system will start doing the math for the intermediate moves that take you from here to there.
Eg if you’re in bed on a cold morning and you want to get up it makes it much easier if you start imagining yourself kicking away your duvet turning on the heater grabbing your warm pants and a sweater and getting started on the coffee whose sweet sweet aroma you’ll be inhaling in a few minutes and once that path becomes high enough specificity your body can just kind of execute it isn’t that wild? That’s manifesting. And active inference.

So setting intentions on processes is smarter than setting intentions on goals because you’re intervening earlier in the active inference loop. Most times you can’t really control goals because you can’t control external outcomes. It seems much more reliable to influence process, which is further upstream in the causal chain. You can just decide what you will do, within your locus of control, and let the chips fall where they may. Not contracting around an outcome even affords you to choose processes that give you options. Processes that are robust to many outcomes.

This is consistent with the way I understand grace - as intervening further and further upstream in the causal chain, with the most elegant and efficient energy spend per impact.

This also reminds me of this concept from Adlerian psychology of separation of tasks, that I saw in Courage to Be Disliked. It’s basically about how it’s bad for you to intervene in other people’s tasks. It’s disrespectful to meddle in someone else’s work, it hurts a child’s development if you preclude its agency by doing their work for them rather than let them struggle at their own pace. But most relevantly, whether someone likes you or dislikes you is very much their task, and you don’t really have a lot of control over it. So in a sense you have control over process (what you do) but not over outcomes (how you’re interpreted, whether people like you).

It feels silly to say because it’s pretty obvious logically, but I was still setting goals and making my new year moodboard around goals and now it’s totally shifted to being around processes. Can’t wait to see fruits from this new tech.

1: Did you know bells have a different overtone series than string and wind instruments? And you can kind of shape it? And that there are indonesian schools of music that use wildly different scales from the western major scale because their main instruments are 2D and so their physics makes for different overtone series which is where the major scale is derived from? h/t hinterlander

You can just decide what you will do, within your locus of control, and let the chips fall where they may. Not contracting around an outcome even affords you to choose processes that give you options. Processes that are robust to many outcomes.

This is consistent with the way I understand grace - as intervening further and further upstream in the causal chain, with the most elegant and efficient energy spend per impact.

This also reminds me of this concept from Adlerian psychology of separation of tasks, that I saw in Courage to Be Disliked. It’s basically about how it’s bad for you to intervene in other people’s tasks. It’s disrespectful to meddle in someone else’s work, it hurts a child’s development if you preclude its agency by doing their work for them rather than let them struggle at their own pace. But most relevantly, whether someone likes you or dislikes you is very much their task, and you don’t really have a lot of control over it. So in a sense you have control over process (what you do) but not over outcomes (how you’re interpreted, whether people like you).

It feels silly to say because it’s pretty obvious logically, but I was still setting goals and making my new year moodboard around goals and now it’s totally shifted to being around processes. Can’t wait to see fruits from this new tech.
